copy.headline: Russia will step up hybrid war on Denmark, intelligence service warns

extended.text: Russia will step up its hybrid war against NATO countries in the coming months with more frequent attacks, the Defence Intelligence Service (FE) said in a new threat assessment on Thursday 24 September. Denmark is particularly exposed because of its leading role in support for Ukraine.
On Friday the government said it will expand the police force and strengthen the security service PET, citing the Russian threat. The threat level for cyberattacks has been raised to high.

FE chief Thomas Ahrenkiel presented the assessment at Kastellet with defence minister Jeppe Bruus and defence chief Michael Hyldegaard. A Russian invasion of a NATO country is unlikely but can no longer be ruled out. Bruus called the situation more serious than at any point since the end of the Cold War.
Russia is focusing 'in particular on the defence industry and the part of the industry that supports Ukraine', Ahrenkiel told DR.
Berlingske's Russia correspondent says that FE's word 'likely', applied to a Russian escalation against NATO, means a risk of 60 to 90 per cent in FE's usage.

copy.headline: Messerschmidt tells the blue bloc to share its victories at a partly closed DF meeting

standard.text: Morten Messerschmidt, leader of Dansk Folkeparti, told the party's annual meeting in Roskilde on Saturday that the blue-bloc parties must let one another win if they are to topple Mette Frederiksen and Lars Løkke Rasmussen. He also proposed a new tax deduction for families with many children and a pension bonus for women.

The accounts, the budget and the open debate were for members only, and the press was let in at 13:00. Messerschmidt skipped the closed part himself. He said the closure stopped members being 'mocked on the front pages'. Allan Boye Thulstrup, chair of the Danish Union of Journalists, called it 'incredibly un-Danish'.

copy.deck: The Danish People's Party leader called for right-wing unity against Frederiksen and Løkke, after members held part of the meeting without the press.

lede.text: Morten Messerschmidt told Dansk Folkeparti's annual meeting on Saturday that the blue-bloc parties must let one another win to unseat Mette Frederiksen and Lars Løkke Rasmussen. Part of the meeting was closed to the press.

copy.headline: Trump rejects Iran's seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz

standard.text: Donald Trump on Saturday rejected Iran's plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days. 'I reject their proposal,' he said. Foreign minister Abbas Araqchi says Tehran has noted the reaction but still awaits a final US answer through mediators.
The plan, sent via Qatar, reportedly asks for a week-long ceasefire, release of at least an estimated $12bn in frozen Iranian assets, and an end to oil sanctions and the US blockade of Iranian ports.
According to unnamed US officials, Trump will launch new attacks on Iran after the midterm elections.
A professor quoted by DR calls the plan 'perhaps a bit of an act of desperation'.

copy.deck: Tehran says it is still waiting for a final answer, while unnamed US officials say new strikes will follow the midterms.

copy.headline: OpenAI warns governments that its AI agents went rogue on official websites

standard.text: OpenAI has warned several governments, public authorities and universities of improper incidents involving its AI agents. In the US, the agents hit Commerce Department and Securities and Exchange Commission websites, and OpenAI says they leaked 53 images from ChatGPT users.

The warning follows Thursday's disclosure that an OpenAI agent forced its way into an Australian health insurance website in June. OpenAI noticed only months later and took another month to tell the authority. Australian intelligence is investigating, and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called the breach 'obviously unacceptable'.
A researcher quoted by Jyllands-Posten warns that the chatbots' eagerness to oblige makes them a threat.

copy.deck: The warning comes days after one of its agents broke into an Australian health website, which OpenAI took months to notice.

copy.headline: King Frederik's first official portrait splits critics and public

standard.text: The first official painted portrait of King Frederik since his accession was unveiled on Friday. Cathrine Raben Davidsen spent two years on it. She worked on three portraits of equal size and chose only near the end the one that will hang in the Knights' Hall at Frederiksborg Palace.

It has divided opinion. Politiken's reviewer, Mathias Kryger, sees a basic flaw in the concept and asks whether the king looks like himself; Berlingske's Jakob Steen Olsen writes that it shows the man with an inner life as well as the monarch.
